en: Composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Kumārila; now begins the second chapter.
I shall now describe the Śravaṇā-rite and the rite known as the Sarpabali. On the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one performs these two rites.
On that day, one should fill a new water-pot with barley-meal (yāvaka) and roasted grain flour (saktu), and place it upon a new sling, along with a ladle made of Vikaṅkata wood.

Having selected a pure place in the eastern direction for the sake of the sacrificial offering, and having separated one portion of barley and grains, he should anoint it with clarified butter. When the sun has set, he should perform the *anvādhāna* and subsequent rites as before. However, the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) and sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of the two oblations are done silently; here, the threshing and other preliminary rites are performed as previously described, after which the rice-grains are divided. There, he should cook a *puroḍāśa* cake with one portion and a *caru* oblation with the other.

In this rite, one should bake the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) on a single potsherd; there should be the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa) for the parched grains (dhānā) together with the clarified butter (ājya).

When the clarified butter has been entirely purified, there should be a threefold sprinkling of those [vessels]. (One should first place the *caru* offering, and after that the *puroḍāśa*). One should immerse the entire *puroḍāśa* in the clarified butter upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), or one should immerse the *puroḍāśa* with its back exposed to the light.

Then, having performed the rites up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings, he should offer four oblations of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*). Following that, he should offer four oblations with the verses beginning "O Agni, lead us" (*agne naya*), reciting one verse at a time. Then, having spread a base of clarified butter (*upastīrya*) with his left hand upon his right hand which has been sprinkled with water, he should place the entire, unbroken cake on a single potsherd (*ekakapāla*) with his left hand. He should then perform the double sprinkling (*dvirabhighāraṇa*) over it with his left hand. Then, with the mantra "To Acyuta," he offers it with his right hand. He offers that [cake] with the dipping-spoon (*sruva*) alone in the clarified butter in which it was immersed.

Above the single potsherd (ekakapāla), [the sacrificer] recites the three verses beginning with "mā no agne" (*RV* 1.189.1–3). Then, another person performs the spreading of the under-layer (upastaraṇa) and so forth, while the householder holds them in his joined palms. He should offer the anointed grains (dhānās) with that [ladle], saying: "May they be auspicious to us. Those grains which are not anointed he gives to his sons and others. Then, having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, he should complete the remainder of the sacrifice—from the *caru* and the grains up to the final sprinkling (pariṣecana). Thus has been described the Śravaṇā-karman; now the principal part of the Sarpabali is being stated. Thus ends the Śravaṇā-karman.
Then, having gone out from the house, he should fill a ladle with the flour-meal (saktu) kept in the water-pot and place it in a pure spot prepared for the day.

Having poured water over it and scattered the meal while reciting the mantra "sarpadevebhyaḥ," no one at all should pass between the offering and himself until the final dismissal. This prohibition against passing through is stated to last until the concluding dedication. He should then pay homage with palms joined together while reciting the mantra "ye sarpāḥ."

Having circumambulated the *bali* offering and sat down behind it, one should recite once the mantra beginning with "sarpō 'si" and ending with "dadāmi. Then, having said, "I entrust this one to you," he should offer [the food] to his sons and unmarried daughters in order of seniority.

Then, for the wife, the mantra "dhruvāmuṃ te" and so forth is repeated here; however, in this case, the name of the son or others should be uttered in the second case (accusative) in place of the word "amuṃ."
Thinking "the Self is indeed eternal," he then entrusts himself [to the deity]. If others perform it for him, he says, "O householders, do not place me in a state of sin.
With that mantra, because there is no formal descent [from the sacrificial ground], one should offer only the *bali* offering; here, acts such as prostration (*namaskāra*) are not required.
Or, one may offer as many *bali* offerings on that very day as there are hours from morning until evening of that same day. Thus ends the *sarpabali*.
